newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: No quick fix seen in Colombian truckers' strike.
newsitem.headline: No quick fix seen in Colombian truckers' strike.

text.p: The leader of Colombia's main truck drivers' union said he sees the strike that began at midnight Saturday lasting at least through the end of the week.
"The problem will continue all week," said Javier Suarez, head of the Colombian Truck Drivers' Association (ACC).

He said the main sticking point in the talks with the government that ended without agreement late Monday was the union's insistence that the government set minimum cargo rates for highway freight by decree.

Business leaders who participated in Monday's marathon round of talks at the Transportation Ministry rejected that demand out of hand, saying it flew in the face of free market laws of supply and demand.

But Suarez said Transportation Minister Carlos Hernan Lopez had approved the idea in a previous round of talks and was legally empowered to set rates that private transportation companies would have to respect.
"We can't go back to work if we don't have rates set by decree," Suarez told Reuters in a telephone interview.

He predicted that negotiations over the key rate issue would continue for "another couple of days" and said it was only after it had been resolved that talks could focus on 18 other issues on the ACC's list of demands to lift the strike.
These include calls for extra payments to truckers waiting to on- and off-load freight and demands for a revision of vehicle licensing fees and highway tolls.
The ACC says it represents 80 percent of Colombia's truckers and union officials say it has virtually paralyzed all road freight since ther strike began Sunday morning.

Port Authority officials confirmed the effectiveness of the work stoppage in remarks to reporters late Monday, saying only a few trucks had moved into or out of the country's three main ports since Saturday. At least 45 tons of imported goods were reported to have piled up on docks in the Pacific port of Buenaventura since the strike began.
Private coffee exporters say the strike could wreak havoc with May coffee export schedules if it lasts more than 10 days.
